bib.title: COMMONSENSEQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge

question: Can a large multiple-choice commonsense QA dataset be built at scale from ConceptNet so that it is easy for humans but hard for current NLU models?
hypothesis: Asking crowd-workers to write questions that separate three ConceptNet targets sharing one relation to a source concept yields questions needing prior knowledge, which current models cannot answer.
contributions: A new QA dataset centered around common sense, containing 12,247 examples.
A new method for generating commonsense questions at scale from CONCEPTNET.
An empirical evaluation of state-of-the-art NLU models on COMMONSENSEQA, showing that humans substantially outperform current models.

method.summary: Subgraphs of one source concept and three target concepts sharing a ConceptNet relation are shown to Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, who write one question per target and add two distractors; a separate worker group verifies questions. Baselines (embedding, LM, NLI, RC, GPT, BERT) are scored on 5-way accuracy.

datasets.name: COMMONSENSEQA
datasets.split: 80/10/10 train/dev/test; random split (primary) and question-concept split (disjoint question concepts)
datasets.source: ConceptNet (32 million triplets; 236,208 triplets after filtering; about 130,000 triplets / 43,000 question sets) plus Amazon Mechanical Turk; licence not stated
datasets.preprocessing: Filtered 22 relations (dropping general ones like RelatedTo and well-explored ones like IsA), concepts over four words or not English, and low edit distance pairs. Workers kept only if at least 75% of their questions pass verification. Each question verified by 2 workers; kept if at least one answered correctly (filters 15%). Web snippets: first 100 Google results for each of 5 question+answer queries (500 per question).

models.name: BERT-LARGE (uncased)
models.architecture: pre-trained masked LM, fine-tuned; [CLS] question [SEP] answer [SEP], softmax over [CLS] states

models.name: GPT
models.architecture: pre-trained LM; [start] question [sep] answer [end], linear+softmax over [end] states

models.name: ESIM (+GloVe/Numberbatch/ELMo)
models.architecture: NLI model with output layer sized to candidate count

models.name: BIDAF++
models.architecture: BiDAF plus self-attention and ELMo, reads 500 web snippets

models.name: QABILINEAR, QACOMPARE
models.architecture: scores over averaged word embeddings; bilinear q W a, or relu([q;a;q*a;q-a]W1+b1) W2+b2

models.name: VECSIM, LM1B-CONCAT, LM1B-REP
models.architecture: untrained: cosine of averaged embeddings; or LM1B (Jozefowicz 2016) probability of question+answer, REP rephrases 5 frequent prefixes covering 35% of dev

training.seeds: learning curves: each data point is the best of 3 runs; main table runs not stated

other.hyperparameters: GPT: same as Radford et al. 2018 on ROC Stories except batch size 10. BERT: same as Devlin et al. 2018 for SWAG. Others tuned on dev; values not given.
other.learning_curve: epochs varied to keep number of mini-batches constant

inference.retrieval: BIDAF++ only: 100 Google snippets per answer candidate

metrics.name: accuracy
metrics.definition: proportion of test examples for which the prediction is correct

baselines: human (5 workers, majority vote, 100 random questions)
SANITY mode: hard distractors replaced by random ConceptNet distractors
eval.protocol: Test-set accuracy; hyperparameters tuned on dev. Human test: 100 questions, 5 non-generator workers each, no qualification test, no master workers.

evidence.quote: Overall, we generated 12,247 final examples, from a total of 16,242 that were formulated. The total cost per question is $0.33.

results.claim: BERT-LARGE is the best baseline on the random split.
results.setup: COMMONSENSEQA test, random split, fine-tuned BERT-LARGE; baseline_value is human accuracy
results.quote: The best baselines are BERT-LARGE and GPT with an accuracy of 55.9% and 45.5%, respectively, on the random split

results.claim: Humans reach 88.9% by majority vote of five workers.
results.setup: 100 random questions, 5 workers each not involved in generation, majority vote, no qualification test
results.quote: Humans obtain 88.9% accuracy, taking a majority vote for each question.

results.claim: GPT accuracy on the random split.
results.setup: random split test, fine-tuned GPT, batch size 10
results.quote: The best baselines are BERT-LARGE and GPT with an accuracy of 55.9% and 45.5%, respectively, on the random split

results.claim: BERT-LARGE scores 63.6% on the question-concept split, easier than the random split.
results.quote: (63.6% and 55.5%, respectively, on the question concept split)

results.claim: With random ConceptNet distractors (SANITY mode) BERT-LARGE reaches 92.3%, so difficult distractors matter.
results.setup: random split test, both hard distractors (same-relation ConceptNet one and worker-written one) replaced by random ConceptNet distractors
results.table: Table 5, row BERT-LARGE, column SANITY (random split)

results.claim: Random split is about five points harder than question concept split across trained models.
results.quote: Performance on the random split is five points lower than the question concept split on average across all trained models.
results.note: Authors' explanation (memorising question concept to answer) is a hypothesis, untested.

results.claim: BIDAF++ with web snippets does poorly, so snippets add little.
results.setup: random split test, 500 snippets per question
results.table: Table 5, row BIDAF++, column Accuracy (random split)

results.claim: BERT-LARGE accuracy by error category on 100 dev examples: high on surface clues, low on conjunction.
results.setup: 100 dev examples, manually labelled, categories overlap; 23.8 is conjunction, 77.7 surface clues
results.quote: in cases where the correct answer needs to meet a conjunction of conditions, and the distractor meets only one of them (23.8%).
results.note: Other categories: negation/antonym 42.8, factoid 38.4, bad granularity 35.4.

results.claim: Extrapolated BERT-LARGE accuracy with 100k training examples is roughly 75%, below humans.
results.setup: dev set, varying training size, best of 3 runs per point; extrapolation read from Fig 5
results.quote: the accuracy of BERT-LARGE is expected to be roughly 75% assuming 100k examples
The total cost per question is $0.33.

results.setup: 2 verifiers per question, keep if at least one answered correctly
results.quote: This processes filters out 15% of the questions.

results.claim: Ten of 122 workers wrote over 85% of the questions.
results.quote: 10 workers formulated more than 85% of the questions.

limits: Human accuracy comes from only 100 questions with no qualification test.
BERT hyperparameters are copied from SWAG; no per-model values (lr, epochs) are reported for the other baselines.
Skills and error analyses use 100 dev examples.
Ten workers wrote over 85% of questions, so style may be narrow.
Random-split difficulty explanation is a stated hypothesis.
The 2019 baselines are dated; later models far exceed 56%.
